meta.blurb: Oswin Pargeter is the most careful man in Bristol, until a rude and wonderful guidebook arrives on his doormat with a holiday he never booked. Now he must cross a very silly galaxy to find a stamp and a way home.
meta.bible: Oswin Pargeter: a careful, tidy accountant from Bristol who loves rules and never takes risks. Mrs Hobday: his unflappable neighbour, who waves at everything. The Guide: a thick, proud, talking book, A Traveller's Guide to Nowhere, 4,000th edition, sniffy but secretly kind. Captain Marigold Plunkett: cheerful retired driver of the space bus, the Slow Dumpling, which travels by going the long way round. Queue Moon: a moon where everyone queues for something they have forgotten. Mizzle: a planet with polite storms that say excuse me before they rain. Haggle-Under-Two: a market where you pay with true compliments. The Library of Unfinished Sentences: a library of half-written books, run by Ms Quill, a tall grey librarian who whispers in commas. The Shy Mountain: a mountain that hides in cloud when looked at. Nowhere: the place between places, where lost things go. Hotel Nowhere: run by Mr Fnorp, a round blue manager who is always almost on time. Clerk Pim: a very small, stern clerk at the Office of Arrivals. Form 7B: the Return form, needing three stamps. Edith Pargeter: Oswin's grandmother, who visited Nowhere long ago and wrote an entry in the Guide. Bristol. Tuesday. Voice and tone: dry, silly, warm and very British; jokes never cruel; nothing frightening.

A1A2: Oswin lived in Bristol, and he liked rules and quiet days.
One Tuesday, a big book fell onto the floor of his house.
The book cleared its throat and spoke in a proud voice.
Oswin said he had not booked a holiday, and the Guide laughed.
A yellow bus landed outside, and Mrs Hobday waved at it.
The bus stamped his hand, and now he was booked.
The bus rose over Bristol, and Oswin held on tight.
Marigold said the bus goes the long way round.
The Guide read about space: mostly empty, and rude about it.
They landed on Queue Moon, where everyone waited in a long line.
Oswin saw a missing form, and the whole queue cheered.
They gave him a badge, and Oswin felt very happy.
Oswin asked how to get home, and Marigold told him.
Next they visited Mizzle, where the storms were very polite.
Oswin gave his coat to a small storm, and it smiled.
At the market of Haggle-Under-Two, people paid with kind words.
Oswin said one true, kind thing, and he got a map.
The map did not show Nowhere, because it was between places.
Marigold said they must go through the Library of Unfinished Sentences.
Ms Quill, the tall librarian, spoke in a soft voice.
One book was crying because it had lost its ending.
Oswin gave the book a kind ending, and Ms Quill smiled.
Behind the door stood a mountain that hid when people looked.
They closed their eyes, and the Guide told them the way.
At the top, the mountain whispered, “Thank you for not looking.”
A gate in the valley said Nowhere, and nobody knew who lived there.
Mr Fnorp, a round blue man, ran the Hotel Nowhere.
The Office of Arrivals was closed for lunch for three days.
Oswin saw lost umbrellas flying like birds over the town.
One jar had his name on it: Sense of Adventure.
The Guide told him the booking was not a mistake.
Oswin was cross at first, but then he was quiet.
Three days later, Clerk Pim said the form needed three stamps.
The first stamp was from Mr Fnorp, but he needed help.
Oswin spent the night fixing four hundred years of mistakes.
Mr Fnorp cried with joy and gave him the first stamp.
The second stamp needed a lost thing, but the jar stayed shut.
Oswin jumped into a flock of lost umbrellas and flew.
The jar opened, and Oswin laughed out loud for joy.
The third stamp needed a found thing, and the Guide spoke up.
The Guide said Oswin's grandmother Edith had lost it here.
Edith's note said, “Nowhere is lovely if you go on purpose.”
Clerk Pim stamped the form, and Oswin could go home.
There was a party, and Mr Fnorp sang very badly.
Oswin made a speech with kind words, and everyone cried.
The Dumpling left Nowhere, and the Guide asked him something.
Oswin wrote, “Go on purpose, and bring a kind word.”
They landed in Bristol on Tuesday, and Mrs Hobday waved.
Oswin wore odd socks and joined a choir.
Next Tuesday, a postcard came, and the Guide said, “Pack.”
B1B2: Oswin Pargeter lived in Bristol, and he was the most careful man on his street. He ate the same breakfast every day and he had never once been late for anything.
One Tuesday morning something heavy landed on his doormat with a thump. It was a thick book with his name on the front, and a note said, “Your holiday confirmation”.
Suddenly the book cleared its throat and began to speak in a grand, sniffy voice. It said that it was A Traveller's Guide to Nowhere, the four thousandth edition, and that he was very lucky.
Oswin explained, politely, that he had not booked any holiday at all. The Guide said that nobody ever did, and that was the beauty of it.
A bus the colour of custard dropped gently into the street with a soft hiss. Out of the window leaned a cheerful woman, and across the road Mrs Hobday waved from her kitchen without any surprise.
Oswin walked out to say that there had been a mistake. Before he could finish, a ticket machine on the bus door stamped the word “Booked” on the back of his hand.
Captain Marigold Plunkett welcomed him aboard and said that the bus was called the Slow Dumpling. Then it rose over the rooftops of Bristol, and Oswin held on with both hands.
Marigold told him that the Dumpling always went the long way round. She said it was far quicker than it looked, though nobody had ever explained why.
The Guide turned to its entry on Space and read it aloud. It said that space was mostly empty, and rather rude about the fact.
Their first stop was Queue Moon, where everyone stood in one very long line. Nobody knew what they were waiting for, because they had all forgotten years ago.
Oswin walked to the front of the line, where a clerk was weeping over a stack of papers. He spotted one missing form at once, and when he filled it in, the whole queue cheered.
The people of Queue Moon gave him a small gold badge to say thank you. The Guide said that it was rare to be thanked in the galaxy, and Oswin felt a warm glow inside.
Later that day, Oswin asked Marigold how a person could ever go home again. Marigold said there was only one way, and that was Form 7B, the Return form, stamped at the Office of Arrivals in Nowhere.
The next planet was called Mizzle, and its storms were extremely polite. Each dark cloud said “Excuse me” before it began to rain, and “Sorry about that” when it had finished.
A shy little storm explained that it had no coat and felt rather embarrassed. Oswin lent it his raincoat, and the storm rained softly and happily all afternoon.
The market on Haggle-Under-Two was full of noise and colour. The Guide explained that nobody used money there, because everything was paid for with true compliments.
Oswin was terrible at compliments, and he stood sweating in front of a stall for ten minutes. At last he told the stallholder that her hat made her look kind, and he was given a map.
Oswin opened the map and could not find Nowhere anywhere on it. The Guide said that was quite right, because Nowhere was the place between places.
Marigold said that the only road to Nowhere passed through the Library of Unfinished Sentences. She did not sound happy about it, and she gripped the steering wheel tightly.
Inside the library, thousands of books stood on shelves with their last pages missing. The librarian, Ms Quill, was tall and grey and she whispered in commas, as if she was always about to continue.
In one corner, a little book was sobbing on its shelf. It had lost its ending, and nobody had ever been able to find it.
Oswin read the last unfinished line and thought for a moment. He added a gentle ending that made the book stop crying, and Ms Quill opened a tall door for them.
The door opened onto a vast, green valley with a mountain at the end of it. It was the Shy Mountain, and whenever anyone looked at it, it hid inside a cloud.
The Dumpling was too wide to pass, so they climbed on foot. They shut their eyes so that the mountain would not hide, and the Guide told them the way.
When they reached the top, a deep and gentle voice came from the rocks. It was the mountain, and it thanked them for not staring at it.
At the bottom of the mountain they found a wooden gate with a crooked sign. It said Nowhere, and under that, in smaller letters, Population Unknown.
Beyond the gate stood Hotel Nowhere, which was run by a round blue manager named Mr Fnorp. He was always almost on time, and he arrived at the door just a moment after they did.
Oswin hurried to the Office of Arrivals, but its door was closed. A sign said that the office was out for lunch and would be back in three days.
With three days to wait, Oswin walked around Nowhere, and he saw wonders everywhere. Lost umbrellas flew like birds, lost keys lay in baskets, and lost tempers sat in jars on a shelf.
On a high shelf, Oswin found a small glowing jar with his own name on the label. It said Sense of Adventure, lost at the age of nine.
The Guide coughed and admitted that the booking had never been a mistake. Nowhere sent a ticket to anyone who had lost something very big and very important.
Oswin was cross for a minute, and he said that nobody had asked his permission. Then he was quiet, and Marigold sat beside him and said nothing at all.

After three days the Office of Arrivals opened, and a very small clerk named Pim looked at Oswin sternly. He said that Form 7B needed three stamps, and that nobody had managed to collect them for a hundred years.
The first stamp had to come from the hotel, and Mr Fnorp promised to give it if Oswin helped him. His accounts were in a terrible mess, and Oswin was the best person for the job.

The hotel had been charging its guests in minus numbers for four hundred years, and nobody had ever noticed. Oswin worked all night with his pencil, and by dawn every column of figures finally added up.
Mr Fnorp looked at the neat columns and burst into happy tears. He stamped Form 7B with a great thump, and then he hugged Oswin for a very long time.
The second stamp had to come from a lost thing, and Oswin knew which one it should be. However, the jar would not open, however hard he twisted the lid.
Oswin had never done anything unplanned, so he closed his eyes and ran toward a flock of lost umbrellas. He jumped, caught a handle, and was carried up over the roofs of Nowhere.
High above the town, the little jar suddenly popped open, and a golden light flowed into his chest. Oswin laughed out loud, a big, joyful laugh that he had not heard in years.
The third stamp had to come from something that had been found. Everything in Nowhere was lost, so found things were very rare, but the Guide said that it could help.
The Guide explained that Oswin's grandmother, Edith Pargeter, had visited Nowhere long ago and had left it behind. It had been waiting for a Pargeter to find it ever since.
The Guide opened to a page in Edith's handwriting and read it aloud. It said that Nowhere was lovely, but only if you went there on purpose.
Clerk Pim stamped Form 7B for the third time and handed it over with a small, stiff bow. He warned that the trip home would be slow, because the Dumpling would have to go the long way round.
That night the hotel held a farewell party for Oswin, and the lost things danced in the hall. Mr Fnorp sang a long song, and he sang it extremely badly.
Oswin climbed onto a chair and gave a speech made only of true compliments. He thanked everyone in the room, one by one, and by the end almost everyone was crying.
In the morning the Slow Dumpling flew away from Nowhere with everyone waving from the street. On the way the Guide asked Oswin if he would write the next entry.
Oswin took out his pencil and wrote a short entry about Nowhere. He wrote that travellers should go on purpose, and should bring a raincoat and a kind word.
The Dumpling landed gently in the street in Bristol, and the clock said it was still Tuesday morning. Mrs Hobday waved from her kitchen, as if he had only been out for the milk.
From that Tuesday, Oswin changed a few small things. He wore odd socks, he joined a choir, and he started to say yes to things that frightened him a little.
The next Tuesday, a postcard from Marigold dropped through his letterbox. It said the Dumpling was waiting outside, and the Guide said that he should pack a bag and bring his raincoat.
C1C2: Oswin Pargeter, an accountant of Bristol, was by common agreement the most careful man on his street, and he took a quiet pride in it. He ate the same breakfast every morning, wore the same grey scarf every winter, and had never once been late for anything, not even his own birthday party. Surprises, in his firm opinion, were nothing more than mistakes that had not yet been noticed by the proper authorities.

One Tuesday morning, something extremely heavy landed on Oswin's doormat with a thump that rattled the letterbox and startled the cat next door. It was a thick, battered book with his name written neatly on the front, and a small note clipped to the cover announced that it was his holiday confirmation. He read it three times to be quite sure, and then he checked the date on the envelope, which was no help at all.

To Oswin's horror, the book suddenly cleared its throat and began to speak in a grand and rather sniffy voice, as if it were addressing a crowd. It announced that it was A Traveller's Guide to Nowhere, the four thousandth edition, and that he was extremely lucky to have been chosen to carry it. Oswin sat down very slowly on the bottom stair and wondered whether he had eaten something peculiar for breakfast.

Oswin explained, with the patient politeness he normally reserved for tax inspectors, that he had not booked a holiday and had no intention of doing so. The Guide replied that nobody ever booked a holiday to Nowhere, since the whole charm of the place was that it arrived without any warning at all. He found this remarkably unhelpful, and he told the book so, which only made it sniff more loudly than before.

Outside, a bus the colour of custard settled gently onto the road with a long, apologetic hiss, scattering a few leaves across the pavement. A cheerful woman in a captain's hat leaned from the window and waved, and across the road his neighbour, Mrs Hobday, waved back from her kitchen with no surprise whatever. Mrs Hobday, it seemed, had seen everything there was to see in her long life, and she was unimpressed by most of it.

Oswin marched out in his slippers to explain, politely but firmly, that there had been a terrible mistake, and that he would be obliged if the bus would leave. Before he could finish the sentence, a small machine beside the door reached out and stamped the word booked on the back of his hand. It would not wash off, however hard he scrubbed it later, and it glowed faintly green whenever he tried to deny it.

Captain Marigold Plunkett, a round and cheerful woman with enormous eyebrows, welcomed him aboard and introduced her bus as the Slow Dumpling. Then the whole vehicle rose with a gentle shudder above the chimneys of Bristol, and Oswin, who was still wearing his slippers, clung to the nearest pole with both hands. His house grew smaller and smaller beneath them until it looked like a tidy little biscuit, and then it vanished into the clouds.

Marigold explained cheerfully that the Slow Dumpling always travelled the long way round, which was, curiously, a good deal quicker than taking the short way. She had never understood the reason, she added, and she had stopped asking questions about it somewhere around her fortieth birthday. Oswin wrote none of this down, although the accountant inside him badly wanted to, and he sat on his hands to prevent it.

The Guide turned grandly to its entry on Space and read it aloud in a ringing voice for the benefit of the passengers. Space, it declared, was mostly empty, extremely large, and frankly rather rude about both of these facts, and visitors were advised to bring a good book and a sandwich. Oswin found, to his considerable surprise, that he was smiling, which was something he had not done at a book since he was seven.

Their first stop was a small grey moon, where thousands of cheerful people stood in one enormous, winding line that stretched beyond the horizon. Nobody could remember what they were queueing for, since the original reason had been forgotten many years ago, but they were all far too polite to leave. It was, the Guide remarked with some pride, a very popular destination, and the queue for the souvenir shop alone was said to be a mile long.

Oswin, who could never resist a muddle of paperwork, walked to the front of the line, where a young clerk was weeping quietly over an enormous stack of papers. Within a minute he had spotted the single missing form that had held up the queue for three hundred years, and when he filled it in, the entire moon erupted in cheers. He blushed to the very tips of his ears, since it was not often that anyone applauded him for something to do with a form.

The grateful people of Queue Moon pinned a small gold badge to his raincoat, and several of them shook his hand with real tears in their eyes. The Guide observed with a sniff that genuine gratitude was very rare in the galaxy, and Oswin, who had not been thanked for anything since the spring, felt a warm and unfamiliar glow spreading through his chest. It was rather pleasant, he decided, and he wondered why on earth he had gone so many years without noticing.

That evening, as the bus drifted onward through the dark, Oswin cleared his throat and asked how a person might get back home again. Marigold told him that there was only one way, a document called Form 7B, the official Return form, which had to be stamped at the Office of Arrivals in Nowhere itself. Oswin wrote the name carefully on the back of his other hand, beneath the stamp, in case his memory should fail him.

Their next stop was a damp little planet called Mizzle, whose storms had the most exquisite manners that Oswin had ever encountered. Each dark cloud murmured excuse me before it began to rain, and apologised handsomely afterward for any inconvenience to the people underneath. The Guide said that it was the only place in the galaxy where one could be soaked and flattered in the same moment.

A shy little storm drifted up to Oswin and confessed, in a trembling voice, that it had never owned a raincoat and felt dreadfully embarrassed about it. Oswin slipped off his own coat and hung it politely over the cloud, which promptly burst into the gentlest and most grateful shower that the planet had ever seen. The whole street clapped and cheered, and a passing thundercloud wiped its eyes on the corner of a smaller cloud.

The great market on a moon called Haggle-Under-Two was full of colour, noise and the smell of frying sugar, and Oswin could not see a single coin changing hands. The Guide explained, with some contempt for old-fashioned money, that every purchase was paid for with a sincere compliment, and that insincere ones were politely refused at the till. Oswin's heart sank down into his slippers, for he had never said a truly kind thing to a stranger in his entire life.

Oswin had never in his life been good at compliments, and he stood perspiring in front of a map stall for a full ten minutes while a queue grew behind him. At last he said, truthfully and in a rush, that the stallholder's hat made her look like the kind of person who would lend you an umbrella, and her face lit up like a lamp. She handed over the map at once, refused all further payment, and then gave him a bag of toffees for the road.

Oswin unfolded the map across his knees and searched every corner, but he could not find Nowhere anywhere on it. The Guide told him, with the air of a teacher addressing a rather slow pupil, that this was perfectly correct, since Nowhere was the place between places and could therefore appear on no ordinary map. Oswin folded it up again, feeling thoroughly foolish, and tucked it into his raincoat pocket next to his gold badge.

Marigold said gravely that the only road to Nowhere led straight through the Library of Unfinished Sentences, and she did not sound at all pleased about it. She gripped the wheel of the Slow Dumpling a little more tightly than before, and she admitted that on her last visit she had been scolded for whistling. Oswin decided, quite firmly and without any argument, that he would not whistle, hum, or tap his feet for the rest of the trip.

Inside the Library of Unfinished Sentences, thousands of books stood on the shelves with their final pages missing and their last lines trailing off into silence. The librarian, a tall grey woman named Ms Quill, whispered entirely in commas, so that every sentence she spoke seemed to promise that something more was about to follow. Oswin found himself leaning closer and closer in order to hear her, until his nose was almost touching her sleeve.

In a quiet corner of the library, a small thick book sat sobbing on its shelf, its pages trembling like the shoulders of a child. It had lost its ending long ago, Ms Quill whispered, and in all those years nobody had managed to think of a way to finish it properly. Oswin felt his own throat tighten, for he knew exactly what it was to carry something unfinished around for years.

Oswin read the last unfinished line aloud and thought for a long moment, because an accountant knows that every column of figures must eventually reach a total. Then he added a gentle ending, in which the small book was found, loved and read aloud by the fire, and the little volume stopped crying at once. Ms Quill, with a very rare smile that cracked her grey face like sunlight on a frozen pond, opened a tall door.

The door opened onto a broad green valley, and at its far end rose a vast mountain, grey and gentle and apparently half asleep. It was known as the Shy Mountain, the Guide explained, and whenever anyone stared straight at it, it blushed pink and vanished at once inside a thick cloud. The only road to Nowhere led over its great grey shoulder, and there was no way for anybody to go around it.

The Slow Dumpling was far too broad to pass along the narrow path, so the travellers had to climb on foot, and they did so with their eyes tightly closed, so that the mountain would not feel stared at. Oswin carried the Guide in his arms, and the book, to its credit, described every step and every stone in a low and steady voice. They climbed all afternoon in complete darkness, step by careful step, and not one of them peeped even once.

When at last they reached the summit, a deep and rumbling voice drifted up from the rocks beneath their feet, and it was the softest voice Oswin had ever heard from anything so large. It was the mountain itself, and it thanked them quietly and sincerely for not staring, which, it said, almost nobody ever managed. Oswin kept his eyes tightly closed and bowed, feeling that it would be rude to say anything more than a plain thank you.

At the bottom of the mountain, in a quiet and misty valley, they came to a crooked wooden gate with a hand-painted sign nailed above it. The sign said Nowhere, and underneath, in smaller and more nervous letters, it added Population Unknown, as though even the town itself was not entirely sure. Oswin straightened his scarf, smoothed his hair, and stepped through the gate with the air of a man arriving for an important meeting.

Beyond the gate stood a crooked and welcoming building called Hotel Nowhere, which was run by a round, blue and permanently flustered manager named Mr Fnorp. He was always almost on time, and he arrived at the front door a moment after the guests, breathless and apologising, and holding a large bunch of keys that did not fit anything. Oswin liked him immediately, because he had never before met anybody who was more apologetic about being late than he was.

Oswin hurried straight to the Office of Arrivals, clutching his hand with its stubborn stamp, but he found the door locked and a handwritten sign pinned to the wood. It announced that the office was closed for lunch and would reopen in three days, which, Mr Fnorp assured him, was a perfectly ordinary lunch by the standards of Nowhere. Oswin sat down heavily on the doorstep and stared at the sign for a long time, quietly adding up the days in his head.

With three whole days to fill, Oswin wandered through the streets of Nowhere, and everywhere he looked he saw things that had been lost. Umbrellas flew above the rooftops like flocks of black birds, thousands of keys lay heaped in baskets, and jars on the shelves were labelled with lost tempers, lost moments and lost sleep. It was the strangest and most beautiful lost property office that any person could possibly imagine, and nobody queued for the lost things at all.

On a high shelf in a dusty corner, Oswin found a small and softly glowing jar with his own name written across the label in careful handwriting. It said Sense of Adventure, lost at the age of nine, and as he held it, Oswin remembered a boy who had once climbed trees and talked to strangers without the slightest fear. He had not thought of that boy for decades, and he was ashamed to find that he had missed him so dreadfully.

The Guide coughed with unusual embarrassment and confessed that the booking had never been a mistake at all, and that it had known this from the very beginning. Nowhere, it explained, sent a ticket to anyone who had lost something large and important, and it was far too polite to point out what the loss was before they arrived. Oswin held the jar tightly to his chest, as if somebody might come along and take it away from him again.

Oswin was thoroughly cross for a full minute, and he said, with much dignity, that nobody had asked his permission before sending him across the galaxy. Then he fell quiet, and Marigold sat down beside him on the bench and said nothing whatever, which was exactly the right thing to say. The rain of Nowhere fell upwards in silver threads, and for a long while the two of them watched it climb the sky.

Three days later the office finally opened, and behind a very tall desk sat a very small and extremely stern clerk named Pim, who inspected Oswin over the top of his spectacles. Form 7B, he announced, required three separate stamps, each one earned in a different way, and no traveller had managed to collect all three in a hundred years. Oswin rolled up his sleeves in the businesslike way that he had always done before a difficult audit, and he asked for a pen.

The first stamp had to come from the hotel, and Mr Fnorp agreed to give it, provided that Oswin could help him with a small difficulty. His accounts were in a catastrophic tangle, he confessed, and for once in his life Oswin was exactly the right person for the job. He ordered a very large pot of tea and a freshly sharpened pencil, and he sat down at the counter feeling quite at home.

Oswin discovered that the hotel had been charging its guests in negative numbers for roughly four hundred years, and the debts had grown so tangled that even the accountant could hardly follow them. Working all night with a pencil, an eraser and an enormous pot of tea, he untied every knot until, at dawn, every column of the ledger added up perfectly. It was, without any doubt, the finest night's work of his entire career, and not a single person in Bristol would ever know.

Mr Fnorp stared at the neat and balanced columns, and then he burst into noisy and entirely joyful tears that ran down his round blue cheeks. He stamped Form 7B with a mighty thump, hugged Oswin for an alarmingly long time, and swore that he would never be almost on time again, only just barely late. It was the first stamp, and it glowed a warm gold on the page as though it had been stamped with a tiny sun.

The second stamp had to come from a lost thing, and Oswin knew at once which one it must be, but the little jar would not open however hard he twisted at the lid. Clerk Pim peered at him with narrowed eyes and remarked that a sense of adventure cannot be unscrewed, only surprised into returning, and that surprising it would require something quite unplanned. Oswin groaned and put his head in his hands, because he had spent a whole lifetime avoiding anything that could not be put in a diary.

Oswin had never in his life done anything unplanned, and so, before he could think better of it, he closed his eyes, ran toward a great flock of passing umbrellas, and leaped. He caught a handle with both hands and was swept high into the air, over the chimneys and the crooked streets, with his coat flapping and his scarf streaming behind him like a flag. It was both terrifying and perfect, and he could not remember when he had last felt so thoroughly and magnificently alive.

High above the rooftops, the little jar suddenly popped open of its own accord, and a stream of warm golden light poured straight into Oswin's chest. He laughed aloud, a huge, helpless and joyful laugh that echoed over the town below, and he realised that it was a sound he had not made in thirty years. Down below, Marigold was cheering at the top of her voice and waving her captain's hat in great circles above her head.

The third stamp, Clerk Pim declared, had to come from a Found thing, and since everything in Nowhere was lost by definition, such items were extremely rare. Oswin was beginning to despair when the Guide coughed loudly from the counter and announced, in a quavering voice, that it believed it might qualify. The whole office fell silent in surprise, and even the clocks on the walls seemed to stop ticking so that they could listen.

The Guide explained, in a quieter voice than Oswin had ever heard it use, that his grandmother Edith Pargeter had visited Nowhere many years before, and had accidentally left it behind in the Library. It had waited patiently ever since for a Pargeter to come and find it, and it had found Oswin's doormat in the end by itself. He had never known that his grandmother had travelled beyond the village where she grew up, and he felt an ache of pride and loss.

The Guide opened itself to a page covered in a familiar looping handwriting, and Oswin knew at once whose it was, because it matched the birthday cards that he had kept in a drawer. It read aloud in a soft voice that Nowhere was perfectly lovely, but only if one went there on purpose and not by mistake. Oswin wiped his glasses on his scarf and found that, however hard he rubbed, they would not stay clear for very long.

Clerk Pim brought his heaviest stamp down upon Form 7B for the third and final time, and then he handed the document over with a small, stiff bow that was, for him, practically an embrace. He warned Oswin that the journey home would be gentle and slow, since the Slow Dumpling would be required, as ever, to go the long way round. Oswin could hardly stop smiling as he folded the precious paper and slid it into his pocket beside the little gold badge.

That evening, Hotel Nowhere held a farewell party in Oswin's honour, and every lost thing in the district came to dance, from the lost umbrellas to the lost keys and the single lost sock. Mr Fnorp sang a long and heartfelt ballad about friendship, which was delivered with great feeling and with almost no regard for the tune. It was easily the best party that Oswin had ever attended, and, to be fair, it was also the first one he had stayed at past nine.

Oswin climbed onto a chair, tapped a spoon against a glass, and delivered a speech composed entirely of true compliments, which he had practised on a small storm and a mountain. He thanked every person in the room by name, remembering something good about each one, and by the end of it a good half of the audience was weeping into their napkins. Even Clerk Pim, who had not wept since a minor misunderstanding in the previous century, blew his nose loudly into a stamped handkerchief.

In the cold bright morning, the Slow Dumpling rose from the street of Nowhere with a crowd of lost things waving from the pavement below it. Somewhere over the Shy Mountain, the Guide cleared its throat and asked, with something very close to shyness, whether Oswin would consider writing the next entry for the new edition. He said that he would be honoured, and that he would try very hard not to make any mistakes in the figures.

Oswin sharpened his pencil with great ceremony, opened the Guide to a fresh page, and wrote an entry about Nowhere in his neat and careful accountant's hand. Travellers, he wrote, should go on purpose, and they should always bring a raincoat and a kind word, for both would be needed at some point along the way. The Guide read it through twice, sniffed, and declared in a slightly cracked voice that it was perfect and should never be changed.

The Slow Dumpling settled gently onto the road outside his house, and Oswin looked at his watch and discovered that it was still Tuesday morning, exactly one minute after he had left. Across the road Mrs Hobday waved calmly from her kitchen window, as though he had merely stepped out to buy the milk. Oswin waved back, laughing out loud, and for the first time in years he did not mind at all that his shoes did not match.

From that Tuesday onward Oswin changed a few small and wonderful things about his life, beginning with his socks, which he now wore in deliberately mismatched pairs. He joined a choir, took a trip to the seaside on a whim, and learned to say yes to invitations that frightened him a little, and he was never again late for adventure. He was still very tidy, of course, since some things never change, but his tidiness now had a pleasant and slightly crooked smile.

The following Tuesday, a postcard from Captain Plunkett fluttered through his letterbox, informing him in large, careless handwriting that the Slow Dumpling was parked outside and in no particular hurry. The Guide cleared its throat from the hallway table and said that he might like to pack a bag, a raincoat and a kind word, and Oswin, smiling, did exactly that. This time he went on purpose, with his raincoat over his arm and a wide grin on his face, and he did not look back once.
